reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: An overlap syndrome combining features of systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis, defined serologically by high-titre anti-U1 RNP antibodies
Raynaud phenomenon and swollen 'puffy' hands or fingers are common early manifestations
Typical features include arthritis or arthralgia, inflammatory myopathy, oesophageal dysmotility, and sclerodermatous skin changes
Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a leading cause of death and must be actively sought even when patients are relatively well
Interstitial lung disease is frequent and warrants baseline and periodic monitoring
By definition antibodies to U1 RNP are present, usually in high titre, while antibodies more specific for lupus or scleroderma may be absent
Renal disease tends to be less severe than in lupus, but membranous nephropathy and other lesions can occur
Management is directed at the dominant organ involvement, borrowing treatment principles from lupus, scleroderma, and myositis
reference.pathophysiology: Mixed connective tissue disease is a systemic autoimmune disorder unified by the presence of high-titre autoantibodies against the U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U1 RNP). B-cell autoreactivity, T-cell involvement, and immune complex formation contribute to widespread inflammation and vasculopathy. Intimal proliferation and medial hypertrophy of small pulmonary arteries underlie the characteristic proliferative pulmonary vasculopathy and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Overlapping mechanisms account for the mixed features of lupus, systemic sclerosis, and inflammatory myopathy, and some patients evolve toward one of these defined diseases over time.
additionalInvestigations: Anti-U1 RNP antibodies and a full connective tissue antibody panel (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, scleroderma and myositis antibodies)
Echocardiography with estimation of pulmonary pressures, escalating to right heart catheterisation when pulmonary hypertension is suspected
Pulmonary function tests with diffusing capacity and high-resolution CT chest for interstitial lung disease
Creatine kinase and inflammatory markers to assess myositis and disease activity
Renal function, urinalysis, and nailfold capillaroscopy
redFlags: Exertional dyspnoea, syncope, or right heart strain suggesting pulmonary arterial hypertension
Progressive breathlessness or hypoxia from interstitial lung disease
Severe myositis with respiratory or bulbar weakness
Scleroderma renal crisis with accelerated hypertension and renal impairment
Digital ischaemia or ulceration from severe Raynaud phenomenon
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally better than for lupus or diffuse systemic sclerosis, but pulmonary arterial hypertension and progressive interstitial lung disease are the principal determinants of mortality. Some patients maintain a mild course while others evolve into a defined connective tissue disease.
pitfalls: Failing to screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension until symptoms are advanced
Assuming benign course and neglecting periodic cardiopulmonary surveillance
Overlooking evolution into lupus or systemic sclerosis over time
Attributing puffy hands and Raynaud phenomenon to a benign cause
Treating with a single-disease framework rather than targeting dominant organ involvement
